segments.script: First, meaning. I read “There I might chance behold / Theseus our captain bold / Meet with the robber band, / Ere they have fled the land, / Rescue by might and…” slowly and put it in my own words: The elders imagine they might, by chance, see Theseus, their bold captain, meet the robber band before those men flee, and rescue the two captive girls. Next, craft. I notice the grammar stays in hope: “might chance behold,” “Ere they have fled,” and “Rescue” is the object of a wish, not a report that the fight is over. The strongest word is “chance”: “might chance” keeps the meeting possible, not finished; the boldness is pictured, not yet witnessed. Then, effect. What do lines 1106–1111 reveal about the rescue imagined? My answer: They imagine the rescue with their minds, still from the grove: confidence in Theseus, and the fact that, for now, they can only sing what they cannot watch.

followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode begins restless and full of questions (“Fight they or now prepare / To fight?”, lines 1126–1127), rises to confidence (“This day shall victory bring,” line 1133) and settles into prayer (lines 1138–1149). The shifting mood lets the audience live through the suspense of waiting, so the sighting at line 1152 lands as relief.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “O when the flying…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from lines 1092–1111 with their connotations, such as “flying foe,” “robber band,” “captives” or “captain bold,” showing how the elders frame Creon’s men as fleeing thieves.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders call Creon’s men “the robber band” (line 1108) and the daughters “the captives twain” (line 1111). “Robber” turns a ruler’s guards into common thieves, and “captives” stresses that the girls were taken against their will. The diction judges the seizure as a crime, not as politics.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The ode’s turn from imagining the fight to prayer, and finally to the sighting of the escort, and its effect: the play moves from danger back toward reunion.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode turns from picturing the fight to prayer: “All-seeing Zeus, O lord of heaven, / To our guardian host be given / Might triumphant” (lines 1138–1140). Its last line turns again, this time into news: “For lo, an escort with the maids draws near” (line 1152). The effect is to carry the audience from fear to certainty and to bring the action back on stage.

items.text: How does “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)” build on “Episode 2 (lines 740–1091)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal link: Theseus left to follow the captors, so the chase happens offstage and the elders, left behind, must imagine it.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Episode 2 ended with Theseus leaving because “the captors speed amain, / While we the victims stand debating here” (lines 1065–1066). Because the chase happens offstage, the elders can only imagine it: “There I might chance behold / Theseus our captain bold / Meet with the robber band” (lines 1106–1108). The departure in Episode 2 causes the ode’s way of seeing.

items.text: In “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the rescue imagined, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about the elders’ motive: they claim to want only to watch, but their prayers show fear for Athens and a wish that their word to the guest prove true.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders say they only want to watch, from above: “And gaze on the fray from the clouds above” (line 1137). Their prayers show deeper motives. They fear for the city, and at the end they turn to the guest and promise that their watch for him was not in vain (lines 1150–1151). They care that the word they gave him proves true.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (What helps people endure waiting for news they cannot control?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer based on what the elders actually do while waiting (imagine, pray, encourage one another), with a line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: My first answer was distraction. The ode suggests something better: shared imagination and prayer. The elders picture the fight in detail and then hand it to the gods: “Hear us, Zeus, and hear us, child / Of Zeus, Athenè undefiled” (lines 1142–1143). Waiting together and naming what they hope for keeps them from despair.

items.text: Where does structure appear in “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”, and how does it connect the rescue imagined to the larger concern with refuge and hospitality?
items.lookFor: Where the ode’s structure (imagined chase, then certainty, then prayer, then the escort sighted) appears, and how it connects to refuge and hospitality: the song ends by reassuring the guest that his hosts kept faith.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The ode is built as a journey: from the battle the elders imagine (lines 1092–1131), to confident prayer (lines 1132–1149), to the sight of the escort (line 1152). Its last lines turn to the guest himself: “O wayfarer, thou wilt not have to tax / The friends who watch for thee with false presage” (lines 1150–1151). The structure ends on hospitality kept: the hosts’ promise, once in doubt, is about to be proved.

items.text: Does the ode make Theseus a hero? Defend your view.
items.lookFor: A defended view: the ode pictures Theseus as heroic and backed by the gods, but it is imagined by people who cannot see, so a counterpoint about praise before the fact belongs here.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: yes, in the elders’ imagination. They call him “Theseus our captain bold” (line 1107) and his men “Dread” (line 1117), and they pray that his host be given “Might triumphant” (line 1140). Counter-line: everything is imagined. At this point the heroism is hoped for, not seen, so the ode makes Theseus a hero only if the next scene confirms it.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): They see it all with their minds, like the blind Oedipus. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines: the elders imagine what they cannot see, but unlike Oedipus they long for physical sight.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: partly agree. They do see with the mind: “a vision rare / Tells me that soon again / I shall behold the twain” (lines 1127–1129). But unlike Oedipus, who trusts inner sight, they long for real sight and wish “To be borne with the speed of the gale” (line 1135) so they could watch. Their mental vision is a substitute they would gladly trade, not a deeper kind of seeing.

items.text: No one acts in “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”; the elders imagine others acting. Whose conduct in the imagined rescue does the ode present as wisest, and whose as least wise? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two figures the ode imagines (Theseus and his riders, the fleeing “robber band,” or the elders themselves), with lines.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of courage in a just cause, the ode presents Theseus and his riders as wisest, charging to bring back “Maidens, the captives twain” (line 1111). The “flying foe” (line 1092) are least wise: they have carried off suppliants from a protected land and must at last turn “to bay” (line 1093). A student could argue that the elders show a different wisdom: they know they cannot fight, and they turn to prayer (lines 1138–1149).

items.text: You are directing “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the rescue imagined.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as the chorus sweeping across the stage as riders or turning as one when the escort is sighted, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) For “Haply on swiftest steed, / Or in the flying car” (lines 1112–1113), split the chorus into two groups that sweep across the stage, as if the elders’ imagination were drawing the chase in front of us. (2) On “For lo, an escort with the maids draws near” (line 1152), have the chorus freeze and turn together toward the entrance while Oedipus, who cannot see, turns a beat late. The audience sees the relief and the blind man’s dependence at once.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 1092–1152: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: Which gods do the elders call on at the end? (Zeus, Athena, Apollo and Artemis, lines 1138–1147.) Why/how: Why do the elders wish for a dove’s wings (line 1134)? (To see a fight they cannot watch.) Should/what if: Should the elders have followed Theseus instead of staying? (Answers weigh their age against their duty to guard the guest.)

items.text: Connect “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)”, with its focus on the rescue imagined, to guilt and intent: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about guilt and intent, the question’s theme. The ode does not argue Oedipus’s guilt; it judges the captors by their acts and intent, so the link is indirect. A strong answer says what must come next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is indirect. The ode does not return to Oedipus’s own guilt; it judges the seizure by its intent, calling the captors “the robber band” (line 1108) and the girls “Maidens so ill bestead, / By their kin buffeted” (lines 1130–1131). That phrase blames kin who meant harm, the reverse of Oedipus, who harmed kin without knowing. To strengthen the link, Sophocles would need a scene where guilt and intent are argued again in person.

items.text: Is the imagery in “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)” effective in presenting the rescue imagined, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment of the imagery against a stated criterion (does it make an offstage battle visible, or pile up names?), with one line that meets it and one passage that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because the images let the audience see an offstage battle: “Flashes each bridle bright, / Charges each gallant knight” (lines 1119–1120) puts the charge in front of us. Counter-line: the long list of holy places and rites (lines 1097–1105) may feel like a catalogue to modern readers. A reviewer might call it heavy-handed unless the class sees these as the sacred sites of Athens’ own land.

items.text: Compare how “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)” treats the rescue imagined with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (people waiting for news of a rescue, in a story, film or real event) and one thing the ode sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Compare a family in a film listening to a rescue on the radio. The ode sees what such scenes often miss: waiting can be an act of loyalty and faith, not only nerves. The elders turn their fear into a prayer for the whole city, “Help with your two-fold power / Athens in danger’s hour!” (lines 1148–1149), so their waiting becomes part of keeping faith with their guest.

items.text: Predict what “Episode 3 (lines 1153–1269)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, the escort sighted with the maids and the elders’ confidence in Theseus, about the next scene, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: “For lo, an escort with the maids draws near” (line 1152), so the next scene will almost certainly open with a reunion. Clue 2: the elders prayed that Theseus’s men be given “Might triumphant” (line 1140), so Theseus will probably come back the victor and Oedipus will owe him thanks. A sharper prediction asks how Oedipus can repay a debt this large.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Stasimon 2 (lines 1092–1152)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the rescue imagined?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: people who cannot act wait for news of a rescue, imagining it and praying, and end by reassuring the person they protect. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Neighbours gather in a kitchen while police chase a car that took two girls from a shelter. They picture the chase street by street, pray, and finally see headlights bringing the girls back. Two things must stay: the group’s imagined view of an action it cannot see (“Might I behold the fray,” line 1095), and its reassurance to the girls’ blind father that it kept faith with him (lines 1150–1151).

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.
